speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to the request made yesterday by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) for whatever figures are available on the number of workers who are working short time and the number who are on temporary layoff. I think the best thing I can do is to refer to the data available in the last monthly report of the labour force survey for December 12, 1953.
The estimated number of persons, outside of agriculture, who worked less than 35 hours-here we take 35 hours as a full week -during the week ending December 12, 1953, was 369,000 in round figures, being 206,000 male and 163,000 female. Of these workers, some 59,000, or 28,000 male and 31,000 female, worked from 1 to 14 hours during the survey week while 310,000, or 178,000 male and 132,000 female, worked from 15 to 34 hours during the survey week.
I should add that there is always a substantial number of people who work on a short-time basis through choice. It is estimated that there were at least 150,000 such people at the time of the last survey.
With regard to persons on temporary layoff, the best information available on these is the number claiming unemployment insurance due to temporary lay-offs. At the beginning of December the number of persons temporarily laid off who were claiming unemployment insurance benefits totalled 13,900.
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), there was no over-all estimate made based on the labour force survey of the number of people working on a short-time basis in the textile industry.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
moved.	i
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers of great war I who hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
He said: In discussing this resolution once again I hope that on this occasion we shall have action taken by the government before the next session is called so that it will not be necessary for me to place this resolution on the order paper again.
To many of the older members of the house this is perhaps an old story, but as we have some 70 new members I think it will bear telling all over again, at least in some modified degree, perhaps.
The Soldier Settlement Act was a piece of legislation that was passed back in 1919, immediately after great war I was concluded. It was passed in a hurry without much consideration and apparently without much knowledge, on the part of those who had to do with the framing of the act, of the conditions that existed. Some 72,000 veterans

of great war I wanted to settle on the land. In my opinion they did not know just what they were trying to let themselves in for. Eventually, 25,017 settlers were set up under this legislation. The total amount of money involved was $109,034,331 which meant that there was an average advance of $4,358.40 made available to each settler. To begin with the interest rate was set at 5 per cent which meant that at that rate it would take only 20 years in order to double their debt. Just as soon as those men went into arrears, the rate of interest was immediately "upped" to 7 per cent and by that very method-in fact by the method of charging them 5 per cent to begin with-the cards were immediately stacked against them.
There was another proposition that did not seem to occur to the framers of this legislation and it was this. While the debt against the soldier settler remained at a certain level, that level was much higher than it should have been because we had just finished a war and as a result had a certain amount of prosperity. But while the debt against the settler was guaranteed, there was no guarantee whatever of the prices that the farmer would receive for his products as the years went by. In this way I believe the settlers were doomed to failure regardless of their suitability for that occupation.
At the time this legislation was brought into effect teams of horses sold for as high as $500 a team. Milch cows sold for anywhere from $125 to $150 apiece. The price of wheat ranged around $3 a bushel and in some cases even higher than that. Of course, that situation was soon taken care of because when the price of wheat, according to some people's opinion, was too high we had a wheat board set up with the definite purpose of reducing and holding down the price of wheat. Before long the price of horses went to a figure as low as $50 a team. In many cases those were only what we used to call crowbait in the first years I was out in that section of the country. Milch cows went down in price to $10 apiece and after a short time we found that wheat decreased in price to a figure as low as 20 cents a bushel at the elevator.
In case anybody should have any doubt about the prices I am giving, may I say that I have here a slip of paper entitled "Authority to Sell Chattel Equipment". This document was issued by the supervisor of the soldier settlement board, Mr. Charles G. Emslie, on December 24, 1924, to a settler whom I know very well; his name is Mr. George Connon. The address here is Islay.
Soldier Settlers
At the present time his address is Hazeldine. I might say that Mr. Connon is one of the men who have been down here on delegations, and now, after a good many years, he owns his farm and has made a good job of arranging for a good set of buildings, fruit trees and shelter belt and all that kind of thing. The description of the chattels given here lists 8 cows. Details are given showing their colour, age and weight. In addition to the 8 cows there is one roan bull 3 years old and two yearling calves. This whole list includes the net amount of $107.50. That means that the 7 cows were listed at $10 a head, 1 at $7.50, the bull at $10 and the two yearlings at $10 each. If anybody wishes to see this document, it is here and may be inspected. There is no question whatever as to the prices I have given. It will thus be seen that the 11 head of cattle that this fellow bought at a price of anywhere from $1,500 to $1,800 was now reduced to the price of $107.50. Many people are wondering why in the world those settlers did not make good. That is one of the reasons.
From the same man I have received another paper. It is an inspection certificate for a carload of oats shipped in 1931. That is before we reached the lowest prices. The carload of oats weighed 2,417 bushels after deduction for dockage, and he received a net price of 16 cents a bushel. It probably cost him 7 or 8 cents a bushel to have that grain threshed. Then he had to pay his freight and other charges in addition, as well as taxes on the land and many other costs in connection with the growing of grain. This illustration again should show people one or perhaps several of the reasons why the farmers were not able to make good under the set-up as originally laid down in the legislation.
There is another matter here that does not look good to me, and I brought it to the attention of the house previously. It is this. In many cases, when the soldier settlement board bought land for resale later to the veterans, the agreement for sale contained the oil and mineral rights. But in 1921, I believe it was, an amendment was made to the Soldier Settlement Act. This amendment took away from the settler and vested in the crown those oil and mineral rights. I remember that about 1938 the then minister of mines and resources, who is now a recipient of some of the good things the country can produce and sits in the other end of this house of parliament, brought in legislation to have those mineral rights restored to their proper owners. The legislation went through the house here without much discussion and,

Soldier Settlers
when it went on to the other end of this building, it was decided there that it should be sent to the banking and commerce committee. I read the Hansard report of what took place. According to it, some of them felt that these farmers were not interested in oil or mineral rights. They said, "They are farmers, so we will just take these rights away". After the matter had been discussed in the banking and commerce committee, it was brought back to the Senate. The report of the committee stated that they should leave the legislation as it was, with the result that the men were again deprived of part of the security which they should properly have had in their agreement for sale. In my opinion, that is a steal from those fellows who went overseas and is something that cannot be forgiven by me or by anybody else who has at heart the interests of these men.
We thought some of our neighbours around the Lloydminster district had a clear-cut case. One of them discussed the matter with me; and at the same time he had a lawyer, Mr. V. U. Miner, who is the mayor of Lloydminster, working on the matter. I remember distinctly coming from Edmonton and riding on the bus with Mr. Miner one evening just before Christmas. We discussed this matter; we thought we had better get our heads together and see what we could do about it. All of the papers were clear and Mr. Miner, a public-spirited lawyer-not of the two-by-four type mentioned here yesterday-stated that he was prepared, if necessary, to give his time and to fight this case through the courts. At that time the Minister of Veterans Affairs was none other than our very good friend, the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). I came down here, discussed the matter with him and told him what we intended to do. I thought it was only fair to do that. He said, "Fair, wait for two or three weeks and we will see what we can do." As a result of his efforts, and without any legislation of which I am aware, the oil rights that had been filched away from these soldier settlers away back in 1921 or 1922, and which had been denied them in 1938 by the gentlemen at the other end of this building, were returned to them. I believe the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was the man mainly responsible for the action taken earlier.
These soldier settlers were not making good and, as I stated before, it was not through any fault of theirs. We remember the conditions that existed in agriculture and in many other industries during the depression years following 1929 and up to the time war again brought prosperity to us in the 1940's. In order to try to keep these debts down to a point where the men could get along without

becoming too badly discouraged, the government first of all brought about a consolidation of loans. Then they decided that the interest rate was pretty high. The interest rate on arrears had been raised to 7 per cent, and the government decided they would cancel the interest charges. That was not good enough, so they decided that the price of the land was too high. To my knowledge some farms in my part of the country were sold at a price four times that obtaining in private sales.
That is one of the things that first of all got me busy on this particular matter. In 1930 there was a 30 per cent reduction in the loans, and in 1936 legislation was introduced giving these settlers the benefit of a dollar for dollar bonus when they paid any of their arrears. I believe all hon. members will recall that at that time conditions were such that people could not make a living on the land, let alone pay off their debts. That system was not working out very well, and in 1938 the legislation was abolished.
The soldier settlers were then allowed to go before the farmers' creditors arrangement board and have their debts reduced. In spite of all the things that were done, and which were considered by many to be very worth while, I want to state that these concessions did not begin to keep pace with the deteriorating condition of agriculture. During all these years these farmers, and particularly their wives and families, suffered privation and want by reason of the fact that they were unable to pay for medical, dental and hospital care. In many cases these settlers or their wives or families passed to the great beyond simply because of the conditions under which they were forced to live.
In the early thirties the price of wheat fell to 19J cents a bushel in my part of the country. Oats went down to 6 cents a bushel, and in many cases it cost 7 or 8 cents to have oats threshed. Cattle sold for a cent a pound, and at that time the dominion government purchased a number of cattle, good, bad and indifferent, at that price. The best hogs that could be raised sold for 2i cents a pound. When taken to market they were turned over at 2J cents a pound. I remember very well that eggs sold at 3 cents a dozen. These prices are not hearsay. Together with the soldier settlers, many of whom were my best neighbours, I went through these conditions.
In spite of the conditions that existed, over which the settlers had absolutely no control, an ambitious director of soldier settlement operations in Ottawa, who it would appear acted without any ministerial supervision

whatever, decided that he would get rid of the soldier settlers who were in debt, probably because he wanted to make a good showing and earn a promotion. They were not paying their debts but they could not do so. He embarked on a program of demanding and getting quit claim deeds to their property and kicked the settlers and their families out on the roadside. In cases where they refused to get out he served them with a thirty-day notice to vacate.
According to figures obtained from the department, in many cases these men and their families were kicked out on the roadside, and the director did not care. I do not think that is the way to treat our veterans who went overseas and offered everything they had, and who were promised that the country would look after them when they returned. But that is what happened. Then there were some of these settlers who were brave enough to enlist after world war II broke out. They decided that here was a chance for them to make a living for their wives and families. Many of them enlisted. Some of them went overseas to different theatres of war and some remained on this side of the water. Of course they could not farm their land while they were away. No provision was made for payment on their debts to the board. What happened? I should like to refer to order in council P.C. 138/1936, passed by His Excellency the Governor General in Council on the 19th March, 1941. Under the heading "Soldier Settlement" it reads as follows:
The board has had under consideration a submission of the hon. the Minister of Mines and Resources reporting that:
1.	A considerable number of persons who agreed to purchase farms from the soldier settlement board or from the director of soldier settlement on long term contracts have enlisted in the Canadian armed forces.
2.	In many cases the dependents of such enlisted persons continued to occupy their farms but no provision has been made for payment of instalments in respect of their contracts or of taxes in respect of their farms.
3.	The director of soldier settlement has no authority to carry such accounts indefinitely and it is considered desirable to provide for deduction from dependents' allowances to cover local taxes and interest due.
They were not satisfied with kicking people out on the road but decided to extract something from the allowances paid by the armed forces to the wives and dependents who were still on the land. The order in council continues:
Accordingly the board recommend that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all cases where the dependents of an
Soldier Settlers
enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement, such deductions to be made monthly and in no case to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was speaking a few days ago in the house I was wishing that it was possible for me to offset some of his fine arguments about the present government's administration by handing him a little bouquet like this. It is a beauty and I think should be preserved for all time to come. I feel that the veterans of the second world war received very good treatment compared with those of world war I. I believe that the exposure of the treatment accorded the veterans of world war I has had quite a bit to do with the treatment accorded veterans of world war II.
In the Western Producer of November 13, 1947, we find this:
In a recent issue "The Legionary" directs attention to an interesting item of news. It points out that the Right Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, Minister of Veterans Affairs, last month presented what he described as "a startling comparison" between land settlement operations under the Soldier Settlement Act after world war I and those under the Veterans Land Act for veterans of world war II.
The figures concerned operations in the province of British Columbia, but it is to be assumed that similar conditions prevail elsewhere. In the year 1925 loaning operations under the Soldier Settlement Act reached their maximum in B.C., as in other provinces. By that year, Mr. Mackenzie said there had been 3,493 loans made under the Soldier Settlement Act, totalling $15,503,474. The average loan was $4,401 and the average loan payable after allowing for 10 per cent down payments was approximately $4,080.
Turning to Veterans Land Act operations, the minister explained that as of July 31 this year there had been 3,030 loans approved under V.L.A. in British Columbia, for a total of $14,720,115. The average loan was $4,094, but the average loan repayable is only $2,027, due to the financial formula contained in the act.
I might state here that instead of the 5 per cent and 7 per cent charge under the Soldier Settlement Act, the veterans of world war II are getting a rate of interest of 3-5 per cent which, in my opinion, is still quite high.
In case I should forget it later on, I might state that there are a number of veterans of world war I who are still on the land, and some in towns, villages and cities, who are not making a very good living. Some of them have their land paid for and some have not. In some cases these men are receiving war

Soldier Settlers
veterans allowances. I should like to refer now to the recommendations in the brief presented by the Canadian Legion to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his cabinet on November 10 last. Two of the recommendations in that brief are as follows:
1.	That the basic rate of war veterans allowance be increased to $60 per month for a single veteran, and $120 for those who are married.
2.	That the ceilings on total permissible income under war veterans allowance be increased to $1,200 per year in the case of a single recipient and $2,000 per year in the case of those married.
I hope these recommendations will be adopted because they have been advocated for many months by members on all sides of the house. I hope that the government will see to it that, in particular, the request for an increase in allowable income will be granted. I believe that request is worthy of consideration. The same remarks apply, of course, to the other request. The granting of the requests will not hurt the government, and it will not hurt many of these people to do some additional work in order that they may build up their income to give them something like a reasonable standard of living.
Time was running out, and many of these old settlers had one big problem on hand before they passed on to the great beyond. This problem was to get a clear title to the land, and be able to leave their wives and families some form of security. These men were all growing older, just as all of us are. Away back in 1936, in the Lloydminster district, a soldier settlers union was formed. Membership was drawn from several other sections of Alberta and Saskatchewan. After some vain attempts to get recognition from any quarter, this organization went out of existence.
In the early forties another organization was formed in Saskatoon under the name of Soldier Settlers Association of Canada. Mr. H. C. Baker was the president and Mr. A. J. Sibley was the secretary treasurer. These two men deserve a lot of commendation for the work they did, particularly Mr. Sibley, who has written hundreds or thousands of letters in connection with this matter. These men received good support here for their demands. I believe they made three trips to Ottawa and made representations to the cabinet and the special committee on veterans affairs. Again I want to express the thanks of the delegation for the courteous treatment they received at the hands of the cabinet and the special committee on veterans affairs. They were pressing for clear titles, and many people at home were supporting their demands.

First of all, these men secured more than 12,500 signatures on a petition circulated throughout the west. They had the support of the Alberta legislature; the Saskatchewan legislature; the farmers' union of Saskatchewan; the association of rural municipalities; the Saskatchewan wheat pool; the united farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section; united farmers of Alberta; Alberta branch of Canadian Legion; the British Columbia branch of the Legion and many other branches, including the dominion Legion command.
After making the final presentation to the special committee on veterans affairs here in June 17, 1948 the committee dealt very leniently with them and gave them a very good reception. I happened to be present. A few days after the delegation left, the committee had an opportunity of discussing this matter. This is the report turned in by the veterans affairs committee under the heading "Soldier Settlement Act".
Your committee recommends that all indebtedness of soldier settlers under the provisions of the Soldier Settlement Act, 1918, be remitted, and that they be granted clear title to their holdings.
That was the report of the special committee on veterans affairs, a committee which has done an excellent job ever since it was set up.

speechtext:
June 17 the representation was made, and this report was turned in a few days later, in June, 1948. This committee was working without any skulduggery or anything of that kind. The committee must be complimented for the work done for the soldier settlers, who greatly appreciate it.
The Canadian Legion presented a brief to the veterans affairs committee on October 26, 1945, and under the heading "Soldier Settlement Act", this is what they had to say:
Therefore be it resolved that, in order to be fair to our aging veterans and to bring the old and the new settlement acts more into line the dominion government be asked to readjust the debts of the 6,153 original soldier settlers who have not paid for their lands, such readjustment to take into consideration the difference in interest rates charged under the said acts; and that following such readjustments the government be further asked to cancel the debts of those original soldier settlers whose debt has been, or may hereafter be, reduced to 25 per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase price.
Later on in the discussion in the committee the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was not quite satisfied with the limitations placed on that recommendation, and at page 315 of the evidence of the committee, October 26, 1945, he had this to say:
On page 11 of the brief there is a reference to the old soldier settlers, and the recommendation

there is that clear title be given provided a soldier reduces his indebtedness to 25 per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase price. X do not think that will go far enough to satisfy the organization that calls itself the Old Soldier Settlers Organization, because they are asking for a clear title for all soldier settlers of the last war. I think we must all agree that the soldiers who are in the most difficult position of all are those soldier settlers who have had no chance of reducing their indebtedness to that 25 per cent, the ones who have been up against bad luck.
Some of you may call it bad management perhaps, but we know that the situation these men went through in the depression years put them in a position where they could not get the money to buy the farm. I should like very much to see that 25 per cent taken out of your recommendation, making it wide open so that title can be given to the old soldier settlers, whether in the fortunate position of being able to reduce their indebtedness to 25 per cent or not. I wonder if Mr. Walker would comment on that?
And Mr. Walker said:
I am sure it will not hurt our feelings if you do give them clear title.
It is quite clear and definite that the people who live in that section of the country and who know the conditions are quite in favour of these people being given clear title. The government, realizing that many of those settlers were in a tough financial position, where they could not get along on their own, decided to make a certain adjustment. For some time the most needy cases were taken care of.
During the past three or four years $150,000 has been placed in the estimates each year, and with that amount of money many of these cases have been cleared up. As of January 1, 1953, the figures show that 548 soldier settlers were still in debt. At January 1, 1954, that number had been reduced to 299, or a reduction of 249 settlers. The total debt of those men as at January 1, 1953, was $572,411.32. At January 1 this year, 1954, it had been reduced to $293,310.90, which means that they are still in debt to an average of $981. During the year, and up to the first of this year, $47,965.71, representing an average of $315.56 each, had been granted by way of reductions to 152 of the settlers.
I might point out that there is still more than $100,000 out of that $150,000 voted by the house still available for the reduction of those debts, and I am suggesting that before the end of the fiscal year, at March 31, the money should be spent in an effort to get some of those fellows out in the clear, so that they can see daylight.
Someone has suggested that they should be given help before a depression hits them. Well, I cannot see any reason in the world for another depression. And if one does come it will be man-made, just as it was back in the thirties.
Soldier Settlers
The government's main objection to granting clear titles is that veterans of great war II will not want to pay up. It says it will wait for perhaps 30 or 40 years, and then will have those debts done away with. In my opinion the conditions under which veterans of great war II have been settled are such that no such condition will develop. If this or any other government should permit conditions which would put those veterans in the same position as veterans of great war I, then we in the House of Commons have a job on our hands, a job of house cleaning, and we will have to do it in a hurry. So far as I am concerned, I shall be ready at any time to help in that campaign.
As I said before, the veterans of great war II have had a pretty good deal. We have yet to rectify the problems of the recipients of war veterans allowances, and should not let many weeks go by before that is done. I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) will give his attention to the matter.
I believe that in Canada we have the best country in the world, and I say that without fear of successful contradiction. We have treated well those veterans of great war II, and I suggest now that we should extend the same treatment to those few remaining from great war I who have gone on the land under the terms set out by the Soldier Settlement Act. Those men have paid everything they could over a period of more than 30 years. As a result of making those payments they have caused themselves and their wives and families to suffer privation and want.
In many cases their machinery and buildings are worn out and dilapidated, and a large amount of money is required these days to replace them. Many of those settlers are doing their best to clear up the debts, but they are hoping at the same time that before they move on to the great beyond they will get clear titles to their homes.
The excessive cost of the things they have to buy today, and the diminishing returns received for farm products, should spur the government to take action before it is too late. Many people do not realize that, because of the high cost of the things farmers have to buy in relation to the prices they receive for their grain, they are getting only about 90 cents a bushel for wheat, in terms of the value of the dollar in 1939.
I am suggesting in conclusion that without further delay, we give these 299 settlers clear titles. I wish to thank hon. members in all parties for their fine co-operation in this campaign on behalf of the old soldier settlers. Incidentally I would point out that I am not

Soldier Settlers
one, myself. Some people seem to think that, because I have discussed this matter on many occasions, I would receive some benefit from having these debts paid off. They will understand that this is not so when I explain that I did not buy any land from the soldier settlement board.
I wish to thank the members of the cabinet and the committee on veterans affairs for the kind co-operation and consideration given by them to the delegation which came here from the Soldier Settlers Association of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few moments of the time of the house to speak on this matter. As the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair) has just said, this is an old story. I remember when I was a boy at school reading the story of the battle of the Nile in which the author said: "It is an old story now, that battle of the Nile-but a brave story, and will never die of age".
The story the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose has told us over a long period of years-some 16 or 17 of them I believe-is an old one. It has also been a brave story, so far as the soldier settlers are concerned, and I hope that, like the story of the battle of the Nile, it will not die of age, but that it will be listened to.
The time has now arrived when the story should be completed. I congratulate the hon. member upon his persistence and his very clear statements of the facts. He has said that there are many new members in the house who have not heard the story about the condition of the soldier settlers, which has continued over a long period of years. It was all to the good that the hon. member should have renewed it today.
I am not going to follow him in all he has said, because I have spoken on this subject on a number of occasions previously. I would also congratulate the Legion, former ministers of veterans affairs, and also the committee on veterans affairs, all of whom have taken a keen interest in this matter.
I do not think the hon. member's efforts have been in vain. While he has not succeeded in obtaining 100 per cent of his ideal, he has received 50 per cent; and as we often say, "Half a loaf is better than no bread". It may not be as necessary to press this matter today as it was some years ago, because considerable attention has been paid to it.
As the hon. member has pointed out, while there were 25,000 who took up land under the Soldier Settlement Act some 35 years ago, today there remain only about 299. I imagine that the number will be less than that and no doubt the minister will give us the correct

number when he speaks. The number has been reduced from 25,000 to that small number. These men owe considerably less than $1,000 on the average. As I said a moment ago, from 1919 to 1954 is a long time. While in the army we used to sing an old song "There's a long, long trail awinding into the land of my dreams". There certainly has been a long, long trail awinding to those who took up land under the Soldier Settlement Act. It has been a pretty rough and stony trail as far as they are concerned. The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair) has outlined many of the difficulties which they encountered.
A great deal of credit is due to those men who have paid for their farms under the most extreme difficulties over that long period of years. Others have not been able to pay in the 35 years. I will not say that there are excuses, but no doubt there are many reasons why they have not paid. Perhaps some of them were poor farmers to start with. I met many men after the first war who had a great love for the land and open spaces and who thought they would like to take up farming. They did not prove to be good farmers and as a result they did not make a success of farming and could not pay for their farms.
There were others who had large families and who located on poor farms and were thus unable to make a living. They also, over this long period of years, were unable to pay for their farms. Certain sections of the country were not well adapted to farming. I have heard hon. members from Alberta tell of men who took up land in southern Alberta and in other dried-out areas of the west. The cards were stacked against those men and in the ordinary course of events they just could not pay for their farms.
The government has been generous in the past as far as these men are concerned, but there are only a few of them left. As the hon. member stated, these men are not young. They have lived most of their lives. Their average age is around 64 to 65 years. Before they pass on to the great beyond they would like to feel that they own the farms on which they have lived for the past 35 years. They would like to hand on their farms to their children, or probably to their grandchildren, the farms upon which they had raised their children and upon which they had spent most of their working lives.
This is practically all I wish to say to the minister this afternoon. These men have worked for 35 years on these farms. I do not think that if we waited for another 35 years we could clean this up and say that the last man has paid for his farm. In the first place, these men will not live that long. I think

the problem has been reduced practically to the irreducible minimum. It seems to me that there would be no better time than right now in this year 1954 for the minister to act. There is only a small amount still owing, I imagine in the vicinity of $300,000, and the minister will tell us the exact amount. I should like to see the minister get up this afternoon and tell us and these few men

I know it is absolutely hopeless for some of them to be able to pay-that the slate is going to be wiped clean.
There is no need of the minister repeating the excuse which has been used in the past that it might be considered unfair to those men who bought farms under the Veterans Land Act or to those old soldiers who have paid for their farms. There would not be one dissenting voice from the old soldiers who have paid for their farms. The men who bought land under the Veterans Land Act received so much better treatment that they would be ashamed to complain of any treatment given to these men.
This is all I have to say. As I said before, I have spoken on this matter time and time again. If the minister is not prepared to take action himself and announce it today, I hope he will take up the matter with his colleagues and before this session is over permit us to write "finis" to this long story of suffering as far as these old veterans are concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great deal of credit is due to the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair) for his great persistence in bringing this matter before hon. members of this house. I was present in the house from 1945 to 1949 and I can remember the hon. member persistently bringing up a resolution similar to the one we are debating today. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers of great war I who hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
There is little need for me to attempt to document the case as the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose has done this excellently. I think all members of the house will agree that the evidence which he has placed before us would indicate that it is expedient for the government to take action to bring justice to those veterans who bought land under the soldier settlement board.
I know that many times I have sat in farm homes in my constituency and listened to veterans tell of how they bought land under the soldier settlement board. Those soldiers made one realize the real problem 83276-95i
Soldier Settlers
these men had and that it is one in connection with which the government should take action.
I recall the debates which took place between 1945 and 1949 in this house and I do not recall one hon. member rising to his feet and contending that these soldier settlers had got justice. I remember on one occasion the then member for Rosthern got up and stated that while he agreed with the sentiments of the resolution he felt it would be unfair to those soldier settlers who had died and for that reason he was going to vote against the resolution.
I wish there were more members in the house this afternoon to have heard the argument of the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose. I am sure all would have agreed with him, and with those of us who are supporting the resolution, that it is time that the government took action in connection with this matter. I recall that in 1945 the number of soldier veterans who had bought farms under the Soldier Settlement Act was in the neighbourhood of 6,000. Through death, and for other reasons, that number has been reduced until as at January 1 of this year it stood at 299.
I should think that, when we have an economy which in 1953 will have produced a gross national output of over $24,000 million, this would be a matter which does not and should not be too large a job to settle.
I believe all hon. members supporting this resolution will agree it should not be talked out. It is my hope it will go to a vote this afternoon and that that vote will indicate to the government that members of this house are in full support of this resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in supporting this resolution I want to add my voice to that of the other members who have paid tribute to the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair), who has for years championed the cause of these men against what has been recognized by those who know the story as a grave and serious injustice.
After world war II there was a recognition in this house of the wrongs, errors and mistakes that had been committed by the administration in handling the affairs of the soldier settlement board, and it was realized that these mistakes had resulted in privation and a good deal of unnecessary suffering among men who had already served their country in the theatre of war and had come back to make their homes in the rural areas of this dominion. In spite of that fact, however, many of these men continue to suffer, and many of them have lost their life's work.

Soldier Settlers
I knew many of them in my own constituency and I want to tell this government of the bitterness that was felt by some of these men and their families after they had been evicted by this government following years of hard work. That bitterness remains in the hearts of many of these men and their families.
The member for Battle River-Camrose started this fight some 15 years ago. If he could have reached the ear of the government at that time a good many hundreds of veterans would have been saved, and a great deal of good could have been done. Today there is nothing left but this belated gesture which, if agreed to, will affect some 300 men. But even this gesture would be a good thing. I am sure it would have the support of every Canadian who knows the story, and the support of the vast majority of the members of this house who know the story.
I plead with the minister to make this gesture this afternoon. Surely he can give some ray of hope to the few men who remain.
The story of the soldier settlement board and the records in this house produced year after year, giving the cost of collecting the money from these men during the days of depression and hard crops, described by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose, show that it cost the government more to administer the department than they collected from the men in these areas. These men were placed under an impossible load; under a debt that wore them out and in many cases led to the loss of their life's work.
If this gesture can be made this afternoon, as called for in this resolution, it will in part recognize the noble work of these men who, are real Canadians, who suffered in the field of battle and came back to play their part as good citizens in this Canada of ours. Such a gesture would do something to restore the faith of many embittered people in the good will of the Canadian people and the Canadian government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my thanks and also the thanks of the veterans in the Okanagan valley to the member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair) for bringing up this question.
We have quite a number of the 299 men who have been referred to now living in the area which I represent. I well remember the time 20 years ago when these men were placed rather hastily on unsuitable land. They had no chance to make a living but they were placed on this land presumably because the government was stuck with it
[Mr. Castleden.l
and had been ill-advised enough to purchase it. Many of them quit after three, four or five years and sought work or land elsewhere. As regards the remainder, as far as the soldier settlement board was concerned, they were left with this problem on their hands. A lot of them were anxious to help and they tried to purchase the land at a lower price from the soldier settlement board. But the board wanted its pound of flesh and they forced these fellows off the land and eventually some of that land was sold to newcomers, aliens who had come to Canada, at a lower price than that offered by the returned men.
I feel these returned men have had a raw deal from the very day they bought this land and they are still getting a raw deal. They will continue in that position until we face this problem. It is not a big problem for it involves less than 300 men and they are men who are for the most part at the age of 60 or 70, or perhaps 75. They are no longer able to cope with the struggle of keeping their land and farms going. The land they hold was never any good in any case and that is why they are behind in their payments today.
I believe the country at large and veteran members of this house are wholeheartedly behind this resolution, and in implementing it we would be giving no more than justice to a group of men who helped this country out at a critical period during the first world war. I hope a vote will be taken. I hope it will be a free vote and that it will serve to indicate to the minister that the time has now arrived when his small valiant band of men should be treated right, as the Canadian people would wish to see them treated.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to add one word in support of the resolution put forward by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair). I am sure that after the case he put up today anything I can say would be in the nature of an anticlimax. Yet I feel it is only right that I should add my voice to that of those who support these veterans in their attempt to see that they get a fair share of the things they should get 'out of this country.
These men sacrificed and fought during the first world war. They came back to settle themselves, make good citizens, and work for the benefit not only of themselves and their families but of their country, and in order to produce things Canadians need. They bought their land at a time of inflation and paid extremely high prices for that land, only to see the bottom drop out of everything

within a very few years. These men fought against droughts, depression, and high rate of interest and they are still trying to pay for their land because they got so far behind with the interest payments during a period when they could scarcely keep their families together let alone pay the interest on their farms.
Many of these men have now paid more than the original cost of the land and they are still in debt. They are getting older. Their ability to produce is getting less all the time and I think there should be some recognition of the efforts these men made during the past 30-odd years in trying to keep up payments and raise their families while at the same time contributing to the welfare of this country.
I know the argument has been used many times that by implementing a measure such as this we would be discriminating against those who had paid up and against the veterans of world war II. I do not think there is one veteran who took land under the Veterans Land Act after the second world war, or one veteran who took land under the Soldier Settlement Act and was able to pay for it, who would raise any objection whatsoever against giving these men clear titles to their land so that they may at least have some sort of security, and have a little bit of property that they can call their own in the twilight of their lives.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE CLEAR TITLES TO VETERANS WITH UNPAID BALANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this discussion on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair), I feel that I would be remiss in my duty as Minister of Veterans Affairs if I did not commend the hon. member for the sympathetic interest he has shown in the matter now under discussion over the last twelve or fifteen years, I believe, that he has been sitting in this house. I think he should be commended for this interest. There is no doubt that he has focused the attention of all hon. members-particularly veteran members-who are interested in the case of veterans of world war I on the situation of the soldier settlers who were settled under the 1919 act.
This matter has been debated every year for some time, and I do not think it is necessary for me to go over the history of the soldier settlement of 1919. I think it is admitted by all those who are acquainted with the subject that the scheme under which these men were settled was pretty much a haphazard one. It was one that was evolved hastily at the end of the first world war. It must be remembered that at that time the
Soldier Settlers
government of the day and the parliament of the day did not have any previous experience on how to handle thousands of men being demobilized in a short period of time and on how to find a proper formula to rehabilitate them into the civilian economy. Because of the haste with which the scheme was evolved and because of that lack of experience, I think there is no doubt that, under the Soldier Settlement Act, many may have been settled under conditions which proved to be too onerous for them to make a success of their endeavour. I think that fact has been recognized.
The fact that these men settled under this act had a very hard time of it during the lean years of the depression, during the twenties and the thirties, I think was recognized by the government of the day. When illustrations are given, as has been done in various instances-and as was done by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose this afternoon -of the actual conditions experienced by some of these settlers, it must be remembered that, rightly or wrongly, that situation existed in the whole of the farming communities in this area at that time. I well remember that, during the course of a debate on a similar resolution, a former member of the house- I think he was the then member for Selkirk, Mr. Bryce-mentioned the sorry plight in which he found himself as a farmer in the area in which these settlers were located. He concluded by saying that probably many of them could not take the knocks as well as he could.
During the course of this debate it has been said that these men should have clear title because they have been paying for so many years. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that fact in itself is not a strong argument.
As we all know, representations are made continuously to have long-term contracts under various loan schemes sponsored by the government, whether in the housing field or in the farm loan field. It could be a strong argument only if the extended term is one which affects a contract whose conditions are too onerous and might be termed unjust.
I submit that debt reduction for soldier settlers has been going on for many years. In fact, it dates back to 1922. The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose will recall that originally there were, I believe, 25,017 settlers and that at that time the investment by the federal government under this scheme was slightly over $109 million. Every few years since then there has been some kind of legislative revision designed to relieve those settlers, by reducing their obligations under the terms of their original contract, by

Soldier Settlers
revaluation or by other adjustments of the sort. As I mentioned before, it was recognized that the terms of these contracts were too onerous under the depressed conditions of the twenties and thirties.
The first of these measures was in 1922. If I may, I think I shall take the liberty of enumerating to the members of this house what has been done since the scheme was originally enacted, because it will put the problem in its true perspective. In 1922, 21,269 settlers benefited by an interest exemption which amounted to $10,270,000.

speechtext:
On the arrears. A few years afterward, in 1925, there was a reduction in the price of livestock effective as at the standard date in 1925. What is referred to as the standard date is the day on which the instalment becomes due. There was a 40 per cent reduction in the price of all livestock sold to a veteran prior to the standard date in 1920 and a 20 per cent reduction in the price of livestock sold to a veteran after that date and prior to the standard date of 1921. That reduction amounted to approximately $3 million. In 1927 there was again a new measure which took the form of land revaluation. It reduced the principal owing by veterans by $7 million and it affected some 7,043 settlers.
In 1929 a new measure, which I believe was implemented in 1930, granted a 30 per cent reduction in principal and interest amounting to $11,300,000, and aided 11,912 settlers. In 1933, three years later, a further interest remission totalled $1,310,000 and benefited some 11,612 settlers.
The next measure to alleviate the difficulties of soldier settlers was introduced in 1933, when the dollar for dollar bonus was instituted. During the period from 1933 to 1939 inclusive this measure permitted a reduction of principal payments by some $2 million and interest payments by $1,500,000, thereby helping some 8,512 settlers. In 1934,

as my hon. friends know, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act came into force, and it was applicable to soldier settlers. Under this act up to 1942 soldier settlers received a reduction in principal and interest commitments of nearly $7 million, and about 2,419 settlers were affected.
In 1942 the entire position of soldier settlement was completely reviewed by a special committee on veterans affairs. It was found that the general position of soldier settlers, as shown in the annual report for 1942, should be investigated. It was revealed that approximately 50 per cent of the settlers were in what could be termed a sound or satisfactory position, and that the other 50 per cent were in doubtful or unsatisfactory positions. To illustrate my point, a detailed analysis of the situation showed that 2,953 settlers had acquired an average equity of 67-5 per cent in their farms, and that 606 settlers had acquired an average equity of 32 per cent. Of those in what were termed doubtful or unsatisfactory positions, 1,078 settlers had acquired an average equity of only 17 per cent, and 2,723 settlers had no equity at all.
The parliamentary committee therefore focused its attention on the latter two classes, and it recommended that further relief was necessary for soldier settlers. An order in council was passed in November, 1942, being P.C. 10/472. It contained two main provisions. One was the reduction of debts of soldier settlers by the treasury board on the recommendation of the director, and the second was the extension of term agreements. The provisions of this order were pretty realistically applied by the director, his officials and the responsible officers in the various districts. For the first time in the history of soldier settlement adjustments were made to meet individual circumstances and set patterns for procedure. The basic approach was to consider the capacity of the individual settler in relation to the estimated productive value of his land.
In the three and a half years following this order in council 2,419 debt reductions went through the books, the write-off amounting to approximately $1,300,000. As the result of this procedure soldier settlers made a good response, and by March 31, 1946, 268 settlers had already repaid their loans in cash. I think that is evidence that the order in council passed in November, 1942, had proved a practical and constructive measure with respect to debt repayment for soldier settlers.
The general position of soldier settlers as of March 31, 1946, showed a total of

4,276 active settlers compared with 7,255 in 1942, at the time the order in council was passed. Their total debt was $4,960,000, with an average debt of $1,160. But the average value of their farms still held at $2,500, based on the 1941 inventory, although that was 1946. In the four-year period between March 31,	1942 and March 31,
1946 a total of 2,621 soldier settlers, or one-third of the total active settlers in 1942, repaid their loans in cash and received title to their farms.
One point I wish to make is that through the application of this order in council not only did a great number of soldier settlers repay their loans in cash and get clear titles, but settlers originally classified as being in a doubtful or unsatisfactory position were able to meet the terms, and many of them also secured clear titles to their land. In other words, the quality did not deteriorate over these years.
In 1948 the matter was again discussed in the veterans affairs committee and in the house. My predecessor, the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), introduced a new policy whereby each year an amount was voted in the departmental estimates to help reduce the debt and give clear titles to the remaining settlers. This has had the effect of reducing the present number of settlers to a very small figure. As a matter of fact, I believe the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) will recognize that the action taken by my predecessor, and which has been continued ever since 1948 has, to a great extent, had the effect which he wishes to achieve by his yearly resolution. I believe I can quote figures which will illustrate this fact.
As of October 31, 1948, when the first order in council implementing the new policy came into force, there were 2,637 active soldier settler accounts with a total indebtedness of $2,842,534.30. On December 31, 1953, that is this last December, there were 299 active accounts with a total indebtedness of $293,310.90. I venture to say that it is possible my figures are already slightly out of date, because negotiations are continuously being conducted with these settlers to get them to agree to the new arrangement.

Of the 2,637 active soldier settler accounts as of October 31, 1948, 1,599 had been granted reductions under the various orders in council. As at December 31, 1953, 1,511 had already obtained title, and 827 settlers repaid their accounts and obtained title without any reduction under the provision of the various orders. At the present time, of those 299 accounts which are left with a total indebtedness of $293,310.90 there are 88 who are already repaying the reduced indebtedness after adjustments had been made. In other words, 88 of them have come to an agreement with the director and are paying under the new conditions. This leaves 211 accounts which are not adjusted.
These 211 accounts on which no adjustment has been made as of December 31, 1953, have a total indebtedness of $205,142.26. Of those 211 accounts 41 are not eligible for a reduction for various reasons, such as the fact that the settler and his wife are both deceased or the settler has sold his farm under a private agreement and it is now impossible for the director to make an adjustment with the settler. This leaves 170 who are eligible. Of the 170, there are 36 who have refused to apply for a reduction, although they have been approached and in many cases it was felt that under the order in council they would be entitled to a reduction. These people have said they would continue under the original terms of their contract until final

Soldier Settlers
payment was made. However, we are continuously reviewing the cases of these settlers who have refused to accept a reduction.
There are others whose cases do not meet the terms of the order in council and who, in the estimation of the director, do not warrant a reduction now. I recall that at one time, I believe when the departmental estimates were being discussed, I quoted a case in answer to a question by the hon. member for Battle River. He thought it was a rather odd thing in that the man had refused to meet his obligations, although he was financially capable of doing so. I agreed at that time that I had possibly quoted an extreme case, but I can assure the hon. member that of the balance of 134 active accounts, the majority are settlers who are now capable of paying and who are in a financial position to do so.
I do not want to go through numerous files and name numerous cases, but I can assure the hon. member that some of these settlers are probably in a better financial position than many of their neighbours in the area. Some of them own another farm and operate two farms. They own farm machinery on which there is no debt. Some have homes in the city in addition to their farms, and spend the winter in the city. I will admit that such cases are limited in number, but the hon. member will have to admit also that the number of cases left is quite small indeed. As I say, it is now 134.

In reply to your letter-
And the number of the letter is given.
-dated April 11 I am afraid I shall not be interested in the proposal you put forward for some years, if in fact I am ever interested in it.
Firstly, it will take the next three years to catch up with the urgent dilapidation-barn, roof, eave-trough, woodshed, veranda, hydro.
Secondly, I am more interested in completing my own payments than accepting quite unnecessarily (in my case) government handouts. I am 66 years old in August, and I am told I shall get the old age pension of $40 a month when I am 70. I am in perfect health, and I intend to stay on my farm, as

long as I live. So do not feel there is any need to worry about making a yearly payment of about $170.
Then he goes on to say that lambing was not good but that the calves were good. This is one of the cases. I will admit they are not numerous but, as I said before, we are dealing with only a hundred odd cases. And because of the circumstances I do feel, although I have the greatest sympathy, as has everyone else in the house, for all these soldier settlers who went through a hard period of their lives on these farms, that the matter has now reached the point where it is a question of a few individual cases. In all fairness to the other veterans and to the taxpayers of this country, I do not feel these men who now are left and who are capable of meeting their obligations should get clear title.
I am quite willing to propose to the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair), who has been such an advocate for these settlers that, now that this matter has reached such small proportions, I am willing personally to go through every one of the files of these 134 settlers who might be able to qualify for reductions and obtain clear titles under the present proposal. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks arising out of the statement made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). He has admitted that the settlers under the old Soldier Settlement Act suffered undue hardship, partly on account of the way the act was drafted at that time and also largely due to the fact that in those days we appointed a number of men who, in reality, were not qualified to act as soldier settlement supervisors. As a consequence of this many of the veterans were saddled with land at exorbitant prices. They also acquired stock of poor quality at exorbitant prices. And so, as a result of these conditions, they had two strikes against them before they started.
The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair) has referred to the difficult situation in which the soldier settler found himself during the depression. The Minister of Veterans Affairs replied that civilian farmers, also, found themselves in the same position. But let me point out to the minister that there

is a vast difference. Soldier settlers, prior to the depression, had been saddled with exorbitant debts as a result of inflationary prices. Civilian farmers, on the other hand, had been benefiting from those exorbitant prices and, as a consequence, had been able to build up a reserve which helped to carry them through the depression.
So there is very little similarity between the two cases. On the one hand you have a man saddled with a heavy debt as the result of high prices, and on the other hand a man who has been able to build up a reserve as the result of those same high prices. So I suggest to the minister that there is no comparison between the two cases.
I speak with some knowledge of what I say, because I was one of those who settled under the old Soldier Settlement Act. I remember well the great difficulties in trying to carry on between 1930 and 1935. As a matter of fact, I think I could say that one of the reasons I am down here in parliament today is because I got so disgusted with the whole thing that I became somewhat hostile to the government of the day, and took a greater interest in politics than I would have done otherwise.
I do not wish to criticize unduly the supervisors of the soldier settlement board. I am frank to admit that during the years I always found them very sympathetic. But they used to point out to me that they were tied down by the rules and regulations under the act, and could not do anything about it. To the extent that they were able to do anything, I always found them most sympathetic. And my remarks about the soldier settlement supervisors of the early period do not in any way refer to the type of men who are on the job today. I know that those men we have today are, in the vast majority of cases, of a very fine order, thoroughly competent to deal with the situation.
The minister has also referred to the fact that many concessions have been made, and I agree with him that many concessions were made. But I remember only too well that those concessions invariably were too little and too late. The government waited until the arrears of interest had piled up to such a point that a settler was discouraged from trying to make any further payments. Then they would come along with a reduction, but that reduction was not sufficient to cancel all the arrears of interest.
Then again, a reduction was made in the amount owing on capital equipment. But due to the fall in prices that reduction was nowhere near the depreciation in value of 8327G-96
Soldier Settlers
that capital equipment. And so I repeat that while concessions have been made to those soldier settlers, they were always too little and too late to deal adequately with the situation.
The minister has said that the purpose of the act was to re-establish these men within a period of 20 years. That was originally its purpose. How long ago is it since these men were saddled with that debt? It is approximately 35 years. That is to say, it has required 35 years to establish many of the men who were supposed to be established, under the act, within a period of 20 years. I think we can say therefore, on that ground that as these men have not become established, due to no fault of their own, there would be every good reason for wiping out the amount of their indebtedness.
The minister has suggested that some veterans who left are capable of paying off their indebtedness, and pointed out that some of them are now living in towns. Well, I know several who are living in towns. Some years ago my attention was drawn to a couple who were living out in a drought area; I do not need to mention the name of the place. I went out there and found a family of a man, his wife and seven children, living on a farm on which no man should ever have been settled. It was nothing but a bunch of sand dunes.
I said to him, "Why do you not get out of here? You will never make a living off this farm." He said, "I am getting war veterans allowance to help me out, but they are deducting $15 a month for rent." All he had was a hovel, a two-room shack to house his wife, himself and their seven children. I suggested that he get off that farm and move to town, and that he would get the full amount of the war veterans allowance. He did go to town, and I made arrangements for him to get a small house there. When he left the farm he was able to get the full amount of the war veterans allowance, and I wish to congratulate the war veterans allowance board upon agreeing that the full amount should be paid.
I do not know what happened to the farm. It stands to reason that no one could make a living on it. No doubt it went back to the soldier settlement board and was included in the list of farms upon which soldier settlers had failed to become re-established. That man is now living in town, but no one can say that he is in good circumstances simply because his financial position has improved to the point where he can have a house in town.
There are many of these old settlers who have moved to the towns because they have

Soldier Settlers
become too old to carry on farming operations. They may have a cheap house in town and have rented their farms. The payments they receive from the rents are being made against the indebtedness. They are living on the war veterans allowance. These men are getting old; some of them are now 70 years of age. Surely instead of insisting that every little bit of money they can get should go to the soldier settlement board those veterans should be in position to put a little money aside to look after themselves in their old age. They have not been able to build up any reserve in many cases.
The suggestion has been made that the giving of clear titles to these veterans would create an injustice to other veterans who have paid. I do not think the minister need be worried on that score. That is not the attitude of the Legion, which has supported the idea that clear titles should be given, although they have not pressed for that. As a veteran I know that I certainly would not feel that way, and I went through a lot of hardship in the thirties. I am sure all fair-minded veterans who find themselves in the fortunate position of having been able to pay off their indebtedness and thus get into better circumstances would not for one minute object to this concession being granted at this late stage of the game. The minister should be prepared to go one step further than he suggests and wipe out the debts still owing by this small number of veterans.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much time because I have taken up quite a little already. I am not sorry for doing that, because I feel that an injustice has been inflicted upon a number of people, and I consider it my duty to see that it is remedied, if at all possible.
I thank the minister for the detailed information he has given the house. He gave the amounts that were wiped out by the different processes. I went into those different items in detail. While a number of concessions were granted, they did not at any time compensate for the unnecessary load that was piled upon these settlers to begin with. That has been my objection all the way along.
I have stated before that in my particular part of the country land was sold by farmers to the government at high prices, and then resold to veterans. I know of one particular case where a man sold his farm to the government at four times the price of other land in the vicinity, and that land was sold back to the farmer's son. I bought some of that land at one-quarter the price.
The same thing may be said about the purchase of farm implements and livestock. I cited some cases and gave particulars, and I think they should satisfy the house or anybody interested that land, livestock and equipment were bought at inflationary prices.

Within a few years prices had fluctuated to such an extent that it was impossible for these farmers to make a living or to come out at the right end of the deal.
The minister has said that he will go through the files. I only wish he had been minister in 1937, when I first brought up this matter. If he had gone through the files at that time he might have prevented a lot of men from being evicted. The minister has made reference to men living in the cities or in some cases on their farms, who are able now to pay their debts. I would tell the minister that that has not been done by the settler alone. If he will investigate those cases he will find that the man's wife and his children-I shall not suggest any particular number-have been working, and after 35 years the farmer has reached the position where he can pay for his land.
I hope the minister will go through the remaining files. In order that his hands may be strengthened in dealing with these 134 people who remain I hope to call a vote.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of amending the Canada Elections Act so as to exclude the holding of a general election during the months of July or August except in a state of emergency.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to stress the last five words of this resolution,

Canada Elections Act
namely "in a state of emergency". By including these words the resolution specifically does not take from any government in power the essential right to call an election should an emergency exist. The purpose of the resolution is merely, under normal circumstances, to regard the hot summer months in the same way we regard the frigid winter months, as being improper times to hold a general election. If passed, the resolution is merely a recommendation to the committee which will be set up to revise the Canada Elections Act. At the outset I would ask a favourable decision of the house because I feel it would certainly be in the interests of succeeding parliaments to do as I have suggested.
The modern concept of free, democratic government depends upon two things. The first is that those chosen to represent the people in legislatures shall be elected by a free vote, and that the conditions of the franchise shall be as universal as possible. The second condition, which is equally important, is that a large percentage of the electorate shall take part in the election so that the candidates who are chosen to represent the people shall in fact be the choice of the majority.
Our system of elections provides that the candidate who obtains the largest number of votes shall be elected to the house whether or not he obtains a majority of the votes cast. All that is needed is a plurality over the other candidates individually. We have rejected-and rightly so, I think-such systems as the single transferable vote and any form of proportional representation. In the 1953 election, as I will shortly show, in a huge number of constituencies in Canada the largest number of electors were not those who voted for the member who now represents the riding in this house but those persons who in fact did not vote. In some cases those not voting actually exceeded the total vote cast for all candidates.
Anything which tends to restrict or prevent an individual vote being cast is dangerous, and the end result is bad no matter whether the steps taken to prevent the vote being cast are of a coercive nature or whether they take the form of encouraging apathy in a general election. We in Canada have been fortunate in that coercive practices have been kept to a minimum. We have not, however, been so fortunate with regard to the overcoming of apathy toward our national problems, and it is this danger which is increased by an election held in the heat of the summer and during the period when Canadians living in urban centres are, by national habit, on holidays.

Prior to the end of the 21st parliament, when the August 10 date for the election was given publicity in a newspaper which is close to the government, the question of apathy was raised in the house by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), to which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) replied that it was more important to see that the electors were at home during the enumeration than on election day because if they were not on the list of electors they would be deprived of their votes.
This argument is both naive and spurious; naive because if a citizen is out of his electoral district on election day he obviously cannot vote no matter whether or not he has been enumerated, and spurious because if an elector is not on the list even a few days before the election he can be sworn in by the provisions of the elections act as recently revised. There was a case in my own riding of York West where the residents of a whole street had been omitted by the enumerators, but thanks to the good offices and efficiency of the chief electoral officer they were put on a special list of electors and thus enabled to cast their votes.

speechtext: It was done. A whole street was omitted but the residents were enumerated, put on the voters' list and cast their votes. We worked all day Sunday to get it done for the voting on Monday. I wish to say now that the chief electoral officer was extremely co-operative. The case involved a street running between two long streets of new houses, and neither the enumerating team on the first street nor the enumerating team on the second street took the trouble to enumerate the cross street. I think this was discovered on the Friday night. Anyway, the officials worked on Saturday and Sunday, got the list printed, and everybody on that street was entitled to vote.

Oh, yes, absolutely legal. Furthermore, if enumeration takes place at a time when many people are away, the enumerators can and generally do, because it is in their interest to do so, find out the names of those persons normally resident in the house which may be vacant and add them to the lists. A family who may be holidaying when the enumerator calls on them can be placed on the election roll and enabled to vote, but if the same family is away on election day they lose their votes.
In a country as subject to the great extent of temperature and climatic variations throughout the year as Canada, climate has a very important part to play in our lives.

It is generally considered inadvisable to hold elections during the harvest period, and it would be obviously wrong to hold an election during the bitter winter months. Both of these periods would deprive large numbers of Canadians of their right to vote. The same holds true of a midsummer election in the months of July or August, particularly for the urban voter, and the results of the 1953 election were nothing short of disgraceful in this regard.
What is equally disquieting, however; is the showing for the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba, where in 1953 the vote showed that in only five constituencies in these three provinces did the elected member's vote exceed the number of citizens registered who failed to exercise their franchise, whereas in 1949, when the election was held in June before the holiday season had really got under way, 36 constituencies returned members to this house whose vote exceeded the unpolled vote.
I propose to deal with this in more detail in a minute. I have worked out for every constituency in Canada for the 1949 and 1953 general elections the number of those who did not vote and the difference between these figures and the number of votes cast for the elected members. I do not ask that these figures be placed on Hansard but I suggest that, if they could form an appendix to Votes and Proceedings and be printed later at the convenience of the printing bureau, it would show every member how his constituency voted and the trend as between 1949 and 1953. I have also worked out a summary of the figures for each province for the 1949 and 1953 elections, and I would ask permission to have these summaries placed on the record.
