speechtext:
The distribution of the
Canadian electorate is approximately evenly divided between urban and rural voters. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the city dweller takes a holiday during the summer months. This is particularly true of the industrial worker, and it has become a common practice for entire industrial plants to close down for a period of two weeks sometime during these months.
The industrial worker in Canada today generally goes on a trip or takes his family out of the hot city to a summer resort or cottage, frequently situated on one of our beautiful Canadian lakes. When he has moved his family or is on a trip he cannot be expected to return to vote, because the expense entailed in bringing his family back from the lake doubles his cost of transportation for his holiday, and this he cannot afford. Therefore, if an election is called while he is on holiday he is disfranchised. There is just no other word for it.
In my own riding the largest aircraft factory in Canada, the A. V. Roe Company, was closed during election day, and there is no doubt the huge majority of the employees were deprived of their vote. There were other industries in the same position. The result was that the vote in York West fell from 75 per cent in 1949 to 61 per cent in 1953, that is of the total electors on the list. I was elected by 25 per cent of the electors on the list in my riding, yet I obtained 42 per cent of the vote cast. This I consider to be far from satisfactory.
However, my position is substantially better than many of the other Toronto and York ridings. The members for the city of Toronto itself obtained only 26 per cent of the total votes on the lists, and in the 7 York seats only 25 per cent of the total electors. Therefore the members who represent Canada's largest city in this parliament only represent really about a quarter of the electors. In other words, there were three times as many people who either did not vote or voted for somebody else as those who voted for the members who claim to represent the various ridings in Toronto and the Yorks.
To put it another way, the unpolled vote in Toronto exceeded the total vote of all the Toronto members by 758,500 votes, or an average of 6,900 per constituency. In the Yorks the figures were 52,530 or an average of 7,500 per constituency. The unpolled vote in both Toronto and the Yorks came to the staggering figure of 337,000, over one-third of a million, and it exceeded the total votes cast for all the elected members by no less than 129,000. In 1949 the members were

Canada Elections Act
elected for Toronto with, a majority of 4,345 over the non-voters, and in the Yorks with a majority of 1,135. Thus it can be seen that the members from Toronto and the Yorks in the 21st parliament had a majority of nearly 10,000 votes over the non-voters, whereas in 1953 this had changed to a minority of 129,000. The percentage cast in Toronto in 1949 was 71 per cent. This dropped to 57 per cent in 1953. The percentage vote cast in the Yorks in 1949 was 73 per cent, and this dropped to 60 per cent in the 1953 election.
The largest non-vote in Canada was in York South, where no less than 28,242 electors failed to vote, and the difference between the non-vote and the vote cast for the elected member was 16,026. In York South the votes cast for the elected member were less than one in five; actually only 19-6 per cent of the electors on the list voted for the member who represents the largest riding in Canada. I may say that the hon. member and I have discussed this; and while I am not speaking for him, of course, I am sure the same conditions obtained in his riding as in mine. In fact I believe the same conditions obtained in all the industrial and urban ridings in Canada.
The situation in Montreal is almost equally deplorable. In 1949 the members elected had a majority of 73,500 over the non-voters, whereas in 1953 this had changed to a minority of 36,236. In other words, in Canada's second city there was a changeover of no less than approximately 110,000 votes. The percentage of votes cast dropped from 67 per cent in 1949 to 59 per cent in 1953. The same holds true for all other Canadian cities.
This condition is particularly bad in Vancouver, where the non-voters exceeded the winners' vote by 29,000 out of a total of 146,000 registered votes. The same condition showed in Edmonton, Calgary and Saskatoon, although the member for Regina did receive a majority over the non-voters. The four Winnipeg ridings were also bad. As a matter of fact, Winnipeg North Centre with 22,000 non-voters or 9,000 more uncast votes than those who voted, showed almost the worst result in Canada. The worst, outside of Toronto and Montreal, was Winnipeg South Centre, with an 11,606 majority of uncast votes. The same situation holds true for Hamilton, Lincoln, London, Ontario county, which contains the city of Oshawa; for Timmins, for Waterloo North and for Wentworth, which is partially in Hamilton.
The province of Quebec, however, has an extremely creditable record and only two ridings outside the island of Montreal

returned members with a vote less than that of the non-voters, that is rural Quebec. In Halifax, interestingly enough, the two members who were returned received an inferior vote to the number of non-voters. So far as I could ascertain that is the first time that has happened in many, many years. St. John's, Newfoundland, was in the same position.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is all I have to say on the question of the urban voter and the summer election. We know the pattern of Canadian life. The average Canadian family, whether they be industrial workers, white-collar men or professional men, take a holiday during the summer. It is a national habit. It is almost as national a habit as the wearing of an overcoat in wintertime. When these people are on holidays they cannot afford to return from the place in which they are spending their holidays to exercise their franchise. The results, compared with 1949, show that the pattern of the 1953 election was deplorable.
However, there is a further disquieting manifestation concerning three out of four of the western provinces. Only in Saskatchewan was the vote for the elected members greater than the unregistered vote.
In British Columbia in only one riding, that of Kootenay West, can a member feel that his vote exceeds that of the absentees, whereas in 1949 not a single riding in rural British Columbia returned a member without a comfortable plurality.
In Alberta only the ridings of Lethbridge, Medicine Hat and Vegreville had a plurality in 1953, whereas in 1949 nine of the ridings returned members with majorities over the absentees. The total vote cast dropped from 69 per cent to 62 per cent. The story is similar or even worse in Manitoba, where the total vote dropped from 72 per cent to 59 per cent and the vote cast for the sitting members over that of the non-voters dropped from a majority of 33,742 to a minority of 62,390, or by nearly 100,000 votes.
In making this analysis, one cannot help but be impressed by the stability of the farm vote, for in Saskatchewan, rural Ontario, rural Quebec and the maritime provinces, with the exception of Newfoundland, the vote both in 1949 and 1953 can be considered satisfactory. However, here also the figures for 1953 show a distinct drop from those of 1949. In rural Ontario, for instance, the winners' vote was greater than the non-vote by 282,000 in 1949, but this had dropped to 123,000 in 1953, or by approximately 160,000 votes. In rural Quebec it dropped from 322,000 in 1949 to 270,000 in 1953. Only in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and rural Nova

Scotia did the vote cast in 1953 compare in percentage with that in 1949. In Newfoundland in 1949 the elected members had a majority of 501 over the non-voters, whereas in 1953 this was turned into a deficit of 8,848.
I have made this rather extended study of the election because I believe it is of the utmost importance to us in Canada. Cynics have said to me, "Why do you worry? You got elected anyway." I consider that to be both a dangerous and despicable argument. To have the support, as I have, of merely one out of every four of my constituents is not a situation which can give me much comfort, yet every member from Toronto and the Yorks is in the same position, as are nearly all members from the island of Montreal, although the situation there is somewhat better than in Toronto, and all members from the larger urban centres in Ontario and British Columbia and practically every member as well from Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia.
Therefore, to say that this parliament is truly representative of the majority of the Canadian people, or that the present government by any stretch of the imagination represents a majority, is extremely far from the facts as they are disclosed by a study of the past two elections. Whether or not the government would have been returned, or whether or not any individual would have been returned, or what the success of the various parties would be is not the question. The question is what percentage of the Canadian people do we in this sovereign parliament really represent. In my view it is a dangerously small minority. I place the blame for this largely on the summer election and the national pattern of Canadian life.
It may be said in defence of a summer election that it is easier to carry out the work of an election in the far northern parts of Canada during the summer than in the spring or fall when the break-up of the ice has to be contended with. This is no doubt true, but the number of ridings so affected would probably be only three or four, as compared with well over a hundred that are affected adversely. In this regard also it is interesting to compare the vote of the far northern ridings in 1949 and 1953. The surprising thing is that very little change is discernible in the picture for 1953, and what change there is is for the worse.
Once a country starts depriving people of their votes, even by holding an election at an awkward time, the free institutions of that country are in jeopardy.
Canada Elections Act
I present this resolution to the house in absolute sincerity. We do not represent a majority of Canadians, as we should. We fail to represent them, not through any act of coercion but merely because an election was held in the summer months, in the extreme heat, when apathy toward political matters was at its height. No matter whether I would have been elected or not, no matter whether any other member would have been elected or not; that is not the problem. The problem is this. We must take such great care of our electoral franchise that when the next general election rolls around the members who sit in this chamber can say, "At least we do represent a majority of the Canadian people".

That kind of weather one year with another is apt to be best of all in the month of July, and the next best month is usually August. It may vary from season to season. I do not think there is much doubt that the slightly larger vote in Newfoundland in 1949 than in 1953 had little or nothing to do with the fact that one election was on June 27 and the other was on August 10. The election in 1949, being the first one after confederation, perhaps excited an exceptional amount of interest. If it would not be unbecoming in me to say so, I might suggest that in 1953 a good many people rather took for granted what the results of the election were going to be, and therefore there was not quite as much interest on that account.
Then the hon. gentleman, still looking from the vantage point, perhaps I should not say of Toronto but of Port Credit, referred to our national habit of taking holidays in the month of August. I have no doubt that in the metropolitan area of Toronto that has become a local habit, and there are many other parts of Canada where it has also become a local habit. But most of the people who go away from Bonavista-Twillingate in July and August do so because they have to earn their living, not because they are going on holidays. There is quite a lot of difference between conditions along Mississauga road and those in other parts of the country.
I know the hon. gentleman would at once rise to correct me if I suggested that it would not be a very great hardship to come back from Muskoka to Port Credit on a nice August day. He would say at once that he was not referring to people who can afford to go to Muskoka but to the industrial workers, especially in those plants which are shut down so that everyone may be on holidays. I think that is a problem.
This is a new problem that we did not face even in 1949. I think it is a problem which ought to be considered by the committee which I trust will be set up next year to look at the Canada Elections Act. I am just expressing here an offhand opinion and do not wish to be considered as committing the government, particularly as the government, in relation to the elections act, has never taken the same kind of position it takes in relation to most other legislation. It has always been understood that the elections act is directly the concern of both sides of the house and that the government has no special responsibility for it except to the extent that the government has on its side, generally speaking, more members than are on the other side.
Canada Elections Act
It seems to me that the right way to tackle the problem is to consider ways and means of providing for somewhat wider advance polling. I know there are great difficulties in doing that, in ensuring that there would not be frauds, that there would be no possibility of double voting and that sort of thing, but I do not think it should just be dismissed on that account. It seems to me that that is a better way of going about it.
I do not agree with what the hon. gentleman said about enumeration and voting. It seems to me a great many people are much more apt to be careless about getting their names on the list than they are about voting. We all know that under the present law enumeration takes place soon after an election is called and there is not yet the degree of public interest that develops later on in a campaign. It is much more difficult to get the individual voter to take his responsibility seriously to get his name on the list, other things being equal, than it is to get him to vote. I feel it is quite as important to make as sure as we can that adequate steps are taken to have the enumeration done at a time when it will be carried out properly, and to take all the other necessary precautions to see that people are encouraged to get their names on the list and that the list is a proper and full list-not too full-as it is to get people to vote.
The hon. gentleman talked about apathy during elections. I think that is a genuinely serious problem. I do not deny it for a moment. But I might just remind the hon. gentleman that there was a municipal election held in the city of Toronto last December for the purpose of electing a mayor and council; and it seems to me, though I do not carry the precise figures in my head, that the vote was under 30 per cent. Twenty-nine per cent is the figure that runs in my mind. It may have been that there were only a few more shopping days before Christmas, or it may conceivably have been that there was not much interest in that election and that the outcome was regarded by most of the voters as a foregone conclusion.
I am afraid, human nature being what it is, that when the 'outcome of an election is more or less a foregone conclusion, then regardless of what you do, short of making voting compulsory, there will be fewer people voting than when the people believe there is a real contest. I believe if we look over the results-and we will be able to do that since the hon. gentleman has gone to a lot of effort, which I think we all appreciate,

Canada Elections Act
to produce figures which will give us a clearer picture than perhaps we had before of what happened in 1949 and 1953-and if we apply to them our knowledge of ridings where most people thought they knew what the result was going to be, and the other ridings where they felt the result was in considerable doubt, it will be found that it was in those in which the contest was lively that the vote generally speaking was higher than in those where it was rather a foregone conclusion.
If I may allude once more to the province of Newfoundland, I am not sure that of the outport ridings the vote was not a little larger in the one where I was a candidate than it was in the other four. I think the answer to that is that in the other four ridings the result was absolutely a foregone conclusion, while there might have been some people who thought that in the case of Bonavista-Twillingate the result might have been in some doubt.

In fact I worked it out, and it was 79-9 recurring per cent. That was on the last figures I was able to get from the chief electoral officer.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: What did Joey promise? I mean what did he foretell?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
Nothing whatever but good government, and I didn't make any promises at all.

There is another reason I find it rather surprising that a member of the opposition should be introducing a motion of this kind, and I think it does great credit to the hon. member for York West that he should be so non-partisan as to do so. I took the trouble to look up the Parliamentary Guide to see when general elections had been held since confederation. I found that elections had been held on more days in the month of August than in any other month. In 1867 the election extended from August 7 to September 20, which means it took place in all but six days of the month of August. In 1872-they wanted to be really sure-it extended from July 20 to October 12. It included every day of August. I do not know whether they voted on Sundays in those days.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: It was an entirely different election.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
On both occasions, if my memory serves me right, the history books tell us the Conservatives won the elections. An election was called in January, 1874, and I have no doubt whatever the date may have had something to do with it, though not very much, and it was on that occasion that the Liberals won an election for the first time.
I skip over the others because there was no other election in either July or August until the year 1930, when an election was held on July 28. If I am not mistaken that was the last occasion on which the Conservative party was returned to office.
So, sir, this would be a self-denying ordinance, if you like, which the hon. gentleman is proposing, and perhaps we on this side of the house should welcome it except that it would tie our hands-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: Give the people a chance.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: -and give the people a chance to put the Conservatives in office once again.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: We would not disfranchise hundreds of thousands of people as you deliberately did.

speechtext:
I think, sir, that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) with his customary good humour and moderation is somewhat imprecise in his use of the term, if I may dare to be so academic as to put it that way after what was said about me the other day by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). Nobody was disfranchised. If there are a great many Canadians who value their holidays more than their franchise that does not mean they were

disfranchised. I think that kind of rather loose talk does not really do very much to improve public regard for our institutions. That is only my opinion and I am a novice in public life, as everyone knows.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: That is, in front of the curtain.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I have done much hiding behind curtains or anywhere else. No matter how embarrassing any question may ever be on which I am called upon to vote in this house, I do not think I shall ever find it necessary to be out of the house when the vote is called.
I want to come back to what I said, at the beginning of these rather disjointed remarks, was in my opinion the most serious objection to this motion. Of course, my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)-if I may take his name in vain when he is not here- would not think this was an objection at all, because he would say that all this resolution says is that in the opinion of the house the government should take into consideration, etc. I would not object to it either, as long as we could be sure in advance that that consideration would be unfavourable. But since there are certain hon. gentlemen opposite who, when a motion has been adopted asking the government to take something into consideration, have a habit of dropping out a few of the words-and I do not say distorting them-but giving the impression to others that some decision was made rather different from the one that was actually made, I think it would be inadvisable to take this kind of risk.
What I am really coming to, Mr. Speaker, is this. If the government did consider this suggestion favourably, or if anyone else did consider it favourably1-and I take it that anybody on either side of the house could introduce an amendment to the elections act; the hon. gentleman could have done so just as well as the government-and if anybody introduced such an amendment and that amendment was carried, I think it would be unfortunate. The reason I think it would be unfortunate is that, while I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that, other things being equal, the month of August is not the best month for an election-I quite agree with that suggestion-I do not think we should deny to ourselves any month of the year, because there are circumstances that are a good deal short of the kind of technical emergency envisaged in the War Measures Act when it might be extremely important to have an election.
There are some hon. members still in this house, although very few, who were here in the year 1926. Neither of those whom I
Canada Elections Act
have in mind happen to be in the chamber at this moment. But in the year 1926, as some hon. members who were not here then will also recall, a government was in office with a majority which, to put it mildly, was somewhat precarious. At any time in the six months between the time that parliament met early in January and the time the same parliament was dissolved on the 1st or 2nd of July, I think it was, it might have happened that that government would have been defeated in the house or that some other compelling reason would have arisen for the holding of an election.
It is true that the election did not come until September, I think it was. I have the date here and I might just as well have it right. It was September 14. I do not think September is as good a month as August for an election. But, at any rate, that election was held on September 14. If, as might easily have happened, sometime in May or June it had become necessary to have an election, I cannot think that it would have been to the advantage of the country or to anyone's advantage to have the campaign drag on for an extra month simply to let people go on their holidays.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: Surely if the government were defeated, that would be an emergency.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman did not define his emergency. If that is the kind of emergency he means, I do not see any point at all in his motion.
In the year 1944 there was a situation which some of us will never forget. There was a situation in this house-I do not want to recall any of the memories-when it might have been necessary to have an election at a time of year which would have been even more unacceptable than is the month of August. I think there might have been no choice but to do so if certain circumstances had arisen, but happily they did not arise.
I do not think we should tie our hands in that way, Mr. Speaker. I believe almost any government we are ever likely to have, almost any government the people of Canada are ever likely to return with a majority behind it in this house, is going to be sufficiently responsible that it would not unnecessarily set an election at a time when it was felt it would have the result of reducing the number of people who could vote. I mean that of hon. gentlemen opposite in all of the groups just as much as I do of the members on this side of the house. Maybe I am naive, but that is my honest opinion. I do not believe any of them would take their responsibility so lightly that they would unnecessarily set

Canada Elections Act
an election at a time when they felt it would have the deliberate result of reducing the number of people who could vote.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext: You mean from now on?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION DURING JULY OR AUGUST
speechtext:
I mean at any time.
Because that has nothing to do with what is before us now, I am not going to enter into a discussion of the reasons which were considered good and sufficient for having the election on August 10 of last year. But I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that while the hon. member for York West says that in many ridings more people did not vote than voted for the successful candidate, that fact does not mean that the result would have been likely to be much different even if a great many more of those people had voted. We have now had a certain amount of experience-whether they are good things or bad things is not the point-with what are called public opinion polls. We have one in this country that I believe is conducted honestly and fairly, and there has been the most extraordinary coincidence, both in the provincial and the federal fields, between their observations and the actual results of elections.
